source: CARDI (2011), "Series on: Rice Cultivation Environment Status in Cambodia / Soil Group Classification / Key Characteristics of 10 Rice Varieties / Simple Seed Purification Method" (Khmer, 25pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, 1st printing 2011); CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: CARDI's soil-specific fertilizer recommendation gives a basal (pre-planting/pre-transplant) dose and one or two topdress doses of urea (46-0-0), DAP (18-46-0) and potassium chloride/MOP (0-0-60), all in kg per hectare, split by rice duration group. For early-maturing, non-photoperiod-sensitive rice (grown in both wet and dry season): Prey Khmer soil — basal urea 20/DAP 25/MOP 50, topdress urea 25; Prateah Lang — basal 25/50/50, topdress 50; Bakan & Ou Rung — basal 50/60/50, topdress 80; Toul Samnang — basal 50/50/0, topdress 100; Koktrop — basal 50/75/50, topdress 75; Kampong Siem — basal 50/0/0, topdress 50; Kien Svay — basal 60/0/0, topdress 60; Krakor — basal 100/50/0, topdress 100; Kbal Popret — basal 85/0/0, topdress 85. For intermediate- and late-maturing (photoperiod-sensitive, wet-season only) rice, the same nine soil groups get: Prey Khmer — basal 10/20/40, topdress 20 then 10; Prateah Lang — basal 10/50/25, topdress 25 then 25; Bakan & Ou Rung — basal 25/25/25, topdress 50 then 25; Toul Samnang — basal 25/50/0, topdress 25 then 25; Koktrop — basal 10/50/50, topdress 40 then 35; Kampong Siem — basal 30/0/0, topdress 45 then 30. Kien Svay is a riverbank soil suited only to early/light rice (no medium/heavy rate given); Krakor is a flood/recession-rice soil and Kbal Popret a long-flooded soil, both used for floating or flood-recession rice rather than transplanted medium/heavy rice, so neither has a medium/heavy rate either. Practical rules that go with the table: drain the field before applying topdress fertilizer; never apply fertilizer while rice leaves are still wet with dew; never apply topdress fertilizer when the field has no standing water or, conversely, when it is too deeply flooded; and never apply topdress fertilizer while a stem-borer moth flight/infestation is active in the field. Beyond fertilizer rates, each soil group also has its own natural deficiency and toxicity profile (see the companion soil-identification entry for the full per-group breakdown): most groups are short of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium to some degree, several (Prey Khmer, Prateah Lang, Bakan, Ou Rung) are also short of sulfur, a few are locally short of magnesium or boron, and iron toxicity is common on Prey Khmer, Prateah Lang, Bakan, Ou Rung and Kampong Siem soils, with zinc toxicity also noted on Kampong Siem and an acid-sulfate soil problem noted on Krakor and Kbal Popret. Nutrient uptake reference (Dobermann & Fairhurst 2000, cited by CARDI): to produce 1 tonne of grain plus its straw, an early-maturing rice crop removes about 17.5 kg N, 3.0 kg P, 17.0 kg K, 1.8 kg S, 80 g Si, 3.5 kg Mg, 4.0 kg Ca, 0.5 kg Fe, 0.5 kg Mn, 0.05 kg Zn, 12 g Cu and 15 g B in total, of which roughly 14.5 kg of the 17 kg K removed is carried away in the straw rather than the grain — a reminder that removing straw from the field (rather than returning it) removes most of the crop's potassium uptake. Two supporting on-farm trial findings: recommended-rate chemical fertilizer trials across 6 soil groups raised yield by 34% (Kampong Siem soil, the smallest gain) to 66% (Koktrop soil, the largest gain) over farmer practice; and a chemical analysis of harvested grain found no statistically significant difference in N, P, K, S, Na, Mg, Cu, Zn, Mn, Fe or B content between grain grown with cow manure alone, chemical fertilizer alone, or a cow-manure-plus-chemical-fertilizer combination — i.e. the fertilizer source did not change the nutrient composition of the resulting grain in these trials. Land leveling is presented as a companion practice to fertilizer management: fields leveled well before planting yielded 5% to 180% more than unleveled fields in the same trials, with an average gain of about 34%, because water and nutrients reach the whole field evenly rather than pooling in low spots and starving high spots.
caveat: Fertilizer rates are cross-checked and identical between both source documents (Khmer table in source 1, matching Khmer and English tables in source 2), so these specific kg/ha numbers are higher-confidence than a typical single-source dense table. A companion cost-benefit table in source 2 (fertilizer cost vs. equivalent-value paddy, by soil group) was NOT extracted here because it is priced in 2011 fertilizer/paddy/exchange-rate terms (urea $25.50/50kg bag, DAP $36/bag, MOP $24/bag, paddy 1000 riel/kg, $1=4100 riel) that are 15 years stale and would mislead if presented as current; only the physical kg/ha rates, which don't go stale, are kept. This is directly relevant to the standing Pailin NPK discrepancy open item and should be cross-checked against it and against any existing SSNM/fertilizer content in the KB for overlap or conflicting numbers before merging.
